answers.reason: A best-first row gives an ordinal ranking: X before W before Y, without numerical utility, reciprocal preference or exclusion.
W X W repeats W and omits Y. A strict complete row must contain each right-side label exactly once.
The rankings compare each person's own options only; they provide no cardinal intensity or interpersonal welfare scale.
A blocking pair consists of participants not currently matched to each other who each strictly prefer the other to the assigned partner.
B prefers W to current X, and W prefers B to current A. A-X does not block because A prefers current W.
B-W puts B and W at their first choices. A would prefer W, but W rejects that deviation in favor of B. Neither unmatched cross-pair improves both sides.
The receiver provisionally holds its preferred new proposer B, releasing A; A then continues from its next untried receiver.
Free proposers are A and C, with A the lower index. A already tried W, so its next untried receiver is X.
W already holds its top-ranked B, so the lower-ranked C is rejected. C remains eligible to propose to later untried receivers.

For strict complete preferences, proposer optimality compares only stable matchings: every proposer receives its best stable partner. It does not guarantee original first choices, unique stability or cardinal welfare.
The two listed pairings differ and both lack a blocking pair, establishing at least two stable outcomes for this profile; side choice can yield different results.
There are sixteen ordered proposer-receiver opportunities. No proposer repeats a receiver, so every run uses at most sixteen proposals, potentially fewer.
